Verdict: ACCEPTThe new common-pool extension is valid under the stipulated complete-source catalogue, support-retention rule, exact ledger, and component restriction. The new chain arguments establish the consumed selections needed at their stopping tiles; the original regular-pair profiles then separate those tiles from every older irregular-pair witness. The signed-floor bound, component refinement, and stated saturation consequences follow.The accepted conclusions are
$$U_0+H\ge 2z+r+J+X,$$

$$\mu\ge n_0-e-\left\lfloor\frac{s-r-J-X}{2}\right\rfloor,$$
and the componentwise refinement in §6. The stronger conclusion that  $U_0=H=0$  fills every original phase- $11$  U endpoint receiver is also correct.There is no blocking gap in the full-cap-to- $L_3$  branch despite its absence from the reported physical fixtures. Its proof is a finite induction of arbitrary permitted length. The necessary distinction is that a full cap starts propagation; it does not, by itself, force every subsequent receiver full. A first nonfull receiver supplies  $L_3$ , and  $H=0$  is what excludes that stopping alternative.1. A nonfull regular receiver is usable only after its selection is consumedThis is the first potential failure point, and §2 handles it correctly.Let an original regular  $2P1T$  receiver have endpoint pair  $p,q$ , original selection  $t$ , and original blank  $b$ . If  $t$  is consumed, then
$$p,q,t\in P.$$
If the receiver is nonfull, its remaining corner satisfies  $b\notin P$ . Since  $b$  neighbors both  $q$  and  $t$ , it cannot be finally selected either.Thus its final endpoint set is exactly
$$P\cap Q=\{p,q,t\}.$$
The endpoint  $t$  has a different original owner from  $p,q$ : it was an original support of the pair owner, whose original endpoint set remains fixed. Hence the tile is an actual mixed  $L_3$  tile.The original pair remains a regular  $2P1T$  profile. Its support count must be read from the original source, even after that support has been consumed. Recomputing the profile using final  $T$  would invalidate the later separation argument.A merely nonfull regular  $2P1T$  receiver need not contribute to  $H$ . Both new route constructions establish consumption before choosing a stopping receiver, so they avoid that error.2. The positive exterior chains necessarily stop before an unactivated terminalFor the normalized positive left leg, the stated receivers are
$$Q_j=\{2j,2j+1\}\times\{0,1\},
\qquad 0\le j<a/2,$$
with original pair
$$\{(2j,1),(2j+1,1)\},$$
selection  $t_j=(2j,0)$ , and blank  $b_j=(2j+1,0)$ .These coordinates include the bar-end receiver  $Q_0$ . Its pair is
$$\{(0,1),(1,1)\},$$
and its selection is  $(0,0)$ , consistently with the unchanged constructor.For a leg counted by  $X$ , choose its first consumed  $t_j$ . If  $Q_j$  is nonfull, §2 supplies an  $L_3$  stop. If  $Q_j$  is full, then  $b_j\in P$ . The next original support
$$t_{j+1}=(2j+2,0)$$
has two persistent occupied neighbors:
$$b_j,\qquad (2j+2,1).$$
The second is its original anchor. If  $t_{j+1}\notin P$ , mandatory retention would leave it selected, violating the degree condition. Therefore
$$t_{j+1}\in P.$$
This induction has the correct final step. The last regular receiver has index  $a/2-1$ ; if it is full, it forces
$$t_{a/2}=(a,0)$$
to be consumed. That point is one of the positive terminal singleton’s two original intratile supports, so the terminal would be activated.The definition of  $X$  excludes this outcome. Therefore every counted leg has a first nonfull stopping receiver, and that receiver is  $L_3$ .The argument follows one fixed original leg. It never jumps into the foreign owner of a consumed support, so cycles in the global source-contact geometry do not create a termination issue. The number of steps depends on the actual finite height, without a height cutoff.Different positive legs have disjoint original receiver pairs. For the two legs of one source, their exterior tile columns are  $\{0,1\}$  and  $\{w,w+1\}$ , which are distinct for  $w\ge6$ . Across sources, original endpoint disjointness applies. Two such routes therefore cannot stop in the same nonfull tile: their two disjoint pairs would require four endpoints.Thus  $X$  injects into actual regular-pair  $L_3$  stopping tiles.3. The phase- $11$  chain normalization reaches the actual terminal receiverThe normalization in §4 is the incoming owner’s frame, rather than the marked positive’s frame. In that frame, the source is
$$U(w,a,b)+(1,1).$$
Its bar occupies rows  $1,2$ , columns  $2,\ldots,w+1$ , and its left terminal is
$$(a+1,2).$$
The left cap
$$Q_{\mathrm{cap}}=\{2,3\}\times\{2,3\}$$
has the three original endpoints
$$(2,2),\quad(2,3),\quad(3,2)$$
and missing corner  $m=(3,3)$ . The subsequent regular receivers are exactly
$$Q_j=\{2j,2j+1\}\times\{2,3\},
\qquad 2\le j\le a/2,$$
with pair, support, and blank as stated in the note.In particular,
$$Q_{a/2}=\{a,a+1\}\times\{2,3\}$$
contains the original terminal  $(a+1,2)$ . There is no missing receiver between the displayed chain and the gate tip.At minimum height  $a=4$ , the regular chain consists of the single receiver  $Q_2$ , which already contains the terminal. Thus the minimum-height case is covered.The right chain is obtained by reflecting columns through
$$c\longmapsto w+3-c.$$
Since  $w+3$  is odd, this preserves the aligned tiling. The same proof applies with height  $b$ , independently of  $a$ . The stipulated tiling-preserving normalization then transports each chain back to the actual source and physical gate.Full-cap propagationIf the cap is full, then  $m\in P$ . Its neighboring original selection
$$t_2=(4,3)$$
has occupied neighbors  $m$  and its original anchor  $(4,2)$ . Mandatory retention therefore forces  $t_2\in P$ .Suppose  $t_j\in P$ .If  $Q_j$  is nonfull, it is the  $L_3$  stop proved in §2.If  $Q_j$  is full and  $j<a/2$ , then  $b_j\in P$ , and  $t_{j+1}$  has the two occupied neighbors
$$b_j,\qquad(2j+2,2).$$
Hence  $t_{j+1}\in P$ .This proves the induction through the terminal receiver.For a gate counted by  $J$ , the stopping alternative exists by its definition:an unfilled cap supplies its original  $U_0$  occurrence; orthe cap is full, but some regular receiver is nonfull, so the first such receiver is reached with its selection already consumed and supplies  $L_3$ .A completely filled chain contributes zero to  $J$ . The argument correctly makes no assumption that a phase- $11$  tip’s own original supports remain selected.This establishes the untested “full cap, then  $L_3$  stop” branch symbolically. It does not establish that such a branch has a complete physical realization.4. Original tips, caps, and regular pairs are not reusedAn occupied marked gate identifies one original terminal endpoint of its phase- $11$  U owner.One original tip cannot own two marked gates: it is one physical vertex in one physical aligned tile, while all original positive canonical tiles are distinct. Thus distinct gates counted by  $J$  identify distinct original tip occurrences.For a common incoming owner, the two distinct tips identify its two different legs. Those legs have different caps and disjoint regular-receiver pairs;  $w\ge6$  separates their tile columns. This explicitly handles the common-owner case. Across different original owners, endpoint disjointness gives the corresponding separation.Consequently:an original cap occurrence is not assigned twice;two routes cannot select the same original regular pair;two disjoint original pairs cannot stop in the same nonfull tile.The  $J$ -stopping pairs belong to phase- $11$  negative U sources. The  $X$ -stopping pairs belong to positive U sources. These are distinct original owners, so the same four-endpoint obstruction excludes sharing between the two route families.The choice of first stop is definite, but injectivity does not depend on different routes having different stopping indices. It depends on their disjoint original pair endpoint sets.5. The new resources are disjoint from every older witnessThe supplied hypothesis about the old assignment is exactly the one needed:Every selected old  $H$  witness has an original  $2P0T$  pair, and its nonfull type is  $L_{2\mathrm{bar}}$  or  $L_3$ .Every new regular stopping tile has an original  $2P1T$  pair.Suppose an old witness and a new stopping tile coincided.If their pair owners differed, original endpoint disjointness would give four endpoints in that tile, contradicting nonfullness.If their pair owners agreed, the fixed original profile of that owner in the tile would have to be both  $2P0T$  and  $2P1T$ .The second alternative is impossible precisely because original selections remain part of the original profile after consumption.This excludes old forced  $L_3$  witnesses as well as old  $L_{2\mathrm{bar}}$  witnesses. It also excludes using an unused second slot of an old  $L_{2\mathrm{bar}}$  tile for a new route: the entire tile is separated from every new stopping tile.Unfilled cap payments are distinct original  $U_0$  occurrences. They cannot coincide with an old or new pair witness:different owners would require three plus two distinct endpoints in one tile;the same owner cannot have both a triple profile and an exact pair profile in that tile.Indeed, an unfilled cap has exactly its three original endpoints of one owner, so it is not an  $L_3$  tile at all.The exact reserve identity authorizes adding  $U_0$  and  $H$ . The proof then uses these actual units once: a  $J$ -route takes either its cap occurrence or its regular-pair stop, while an  $X$ -route takes its regular-pair stop. It does not retain the selected cap as a separate unused subtotal after charging it to  $J$ .Combining these routes with the accepted old assignment therefore gives
$$\boxed{U_0+H\ge2z+r+J+X.}
\tag{4}$$
No full-tile credit is added. A full cap or receiver serves only to force the next consumption; it is never itself charged as a new unit.6. Signed parity and the sufficient criterion are correctSet
$$d=s-r-J-X.$$
There is no reason for  $d$  to be nonnegative, and the proof does not require that.Using (4), the exact identity, and  $A\ge s+2t$ ,
$$\begin{aligned}
2R
&=A+U_0+Z_0+H\\
&\ge s+2t+2z+r+J+X\\
&=2(z+s+t)-d.
\end{aligned}$$
The original source ledger supplies  $R\in\mathbb Z$ . Hence
$$R\ge z+s+t-\left\lfloor\frac d2\right\rfloor.$$
Substituting  $n_2=z+s+t+e$  yields
$$\boxed{\displaystyle
\mu\ge n_0-e-\left\lfloor\frac{s-r-J-X}{2}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{5}$$
The floor must remain signed. For example,  $d=-1$  gives
$$\left\lfloor-\frac12\right\rfloor=-1,$$
so (5) supplies one additional unit in the margin. Truncating  $d$  at zero would lose this valid consequence of ledger integrality.For arbitrary integers  $d$  and  $m$ ,
$$\left\lfloor\frac d2\right\rfloor\le m
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d\le2m+1.$$
Taking  $m=n_0-e$ , the displayed lower bound is nonnegative exactly when
$$\boxed{s+2e\le2n_0+r+J+X+1.}
\tag{6}$$
Thus (6) is equivalent to the nonnegativity of this sufficient lower bound. It is not asserted to be necessary for the actual condition  $\mu\ge0$ : unused capacity in  $A,U_0,Z_0,H$  can make the actual margin larger.With the other counts fixed, increasing  $J+X$  by two raises the lower bound (5) by exactly one, including for negative residuals. The note’s “at least one” statement is therefore valid.7. Routes and their resources remain in one endpoint componentThe component restriction has the necessary geometric support.First, the occupied gate of a  $J$ -route is adjacent to persistent endpoints of the marked positive. The incoming phase- $11$  source and that positive therefore lie in the same actual endpoint component.Along either route, a consumed selection is a foreign endpoint adjacent to its persistent original anchor. Its owner consequently joins the same endpoint component. A full cap or regular receiver is likewise connected through endpoint adjacency. All original endpoint pairs and caps along the route belong to the one complete source being followed.These facts also preserve fullness and consumption after restriction:a foreign endpoint filling a cap is adjacent to the original triple;a foreign endpoint consuming a displayed selection is adjacent to its original anchor;any endpoint completing one of the regular receivers is adjacent to its original pair.Such endpoints cannot disappear into a different endpoint component when the complete-source restriction is applied. Conversely, an absent endpoint globally remains absent after restriction.Thus the restriction preserves the conditions defining  $J$  and  $X$ , as well as the already accepted source counts and old witnesses.The sum in §6 is a sum of source margins, using the accepted additive source ledger. It does not add half-areas of component bounding rectangles. Source charges and original events are additive; a full endpoint tile also belongs to a single endpoint component.For
$$d_c=s_c-r_c-J_c-X_c,$$
the componentwise result is therefore
$$\boxed{\displaystyle
\mu\ge n_0-e-\sum_c\left\lfloor\frac{d_c}{2}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{7}$$
The component parity gain works for negative residualsWrite
$$d_c=2q_c+\varepsilon_c,
\qquad
q_c=\left\lfloor\frac{d_c}{2}\right\rfloor,
\qquad
\varepsilon_c\in\{0,1\}.$$
This is valid for negative integers as well. If  $o=\sum_c\varepsilon_c$  counts the odd residuals, then
$$\left\lfloor\frac{\sum_c d_c}{2}\right\rfloor
=
\sum_c\left\lfloor\frac{d_c}{2}\right\rfloor
+\left\lfloor\frac o2\right\rfloor.$$
Hence (7) improves the corresponding global lower bound by exactly
$$\left\lfloor\frac o2\right\rfloor.$$
For instance, two residuals  $d_1=d_2=-1$  have component floors summing to  $-2$ , whereas their combined residual has floor  $-1$ . The improvement is one, as claimed. It comes from separate integer ledgers, with no additional physical resource assigned.8. The saturated  $A+A$  conclusions followFor a failing nonexceptional  $R=1$  component, the accepted census gives
$$n_0=z=t=0,\qquad s=2,\qquad A=2,
\qquad U_0=Z_0=H=0.$$
Equation (4) then forces
$$r=J=X=0.$$
The stated consequences are valid:Every actual marked gate with a phase- $11$  terminal owner has a completely filled associated chain. Otherwise it would be counted by  $J$ . This includes gates on one-mark positives and activated sides, because the definition of  $J$  includes them.No unactivated positive leg has a consumed exterior regular selection. Such a leg would be counted by  $X$ .Any consumed positive exterior chain propagates to an activated positive terminal. Here  $H=0$  is also relevant: it excludes an intervening  $L_3$  stop. The chain therefore reaches and consumes its terminal selection.There are exactly two activated positive-terminal occurrences in this component, already belonging to the two double-marked positives. Therefore the positive exterior chains in item 3 reach one of those two occurrences.The word positive should remain explicit in “positive exterior chain.” These statements do not describe arbitrary negative-source exterior chains or route those chains to the positive  $A$  occurrences.The previous width-six gap-at-least-six and short width-eight/ten transverse-gate restrictions remain unchanged. The new result adds full-chain restrictions throughout the component; it does not turn the residual allocation candidate into an ambient-grid counterexample.9. The source-wide phase- $11$  saturation claim is exhaustiveThe stronger claim under
$$U_0=H=0$$
does not require that a phase- $11$  source own a marked gate. Each of its caps can be used as the starting point of the same propagation argument.To check that “every receiver” is justified, the complete phase- $11$  endpoint-receiver inventory is:Original receivers of  $U(w,a,b)+(1,1)$ NumberOriginal profileBar tiles in row block  $\{0,1\}$  $w/2$  $2P0T$ Interior bar tiles in row block  $\{2,3\}$  $w/2-2$  $2P0T$ Left and right caps $2$  $3P0T$ Left regular stem chain $a/2-1$  $2P1T$ Right regular stem chain $b/2-1$  $2P1T$ This follows directly from the complete endpoint set and aligned tiling. The  $w-2$  bar pairs account for  $2w-4$  irregular endpoints, consistently with the supplied phase- $11$  catalogue. There is no additional singleton or four-endpoint original receiver to handle.Now: $U_0=0$  fills both caps.Starting from a full cap, propagation consumes the first regular selection. A nonfull receiver would then be  $L_3$ , prohibited by  $H=0$ . Induction fills every regular receiver through the terminal.Every original  $2P0T$  bar receiver is full: with only its pair it would contribute  $L_{2\mathrm{bar}}$ , and with one added endpoint it would contribute  $L_3$ .The inventory is exhaustive, so every original phase- $11$  U endpoint-containing receiver is full.This does not assert fullness of a zero-endpoint tile merely containing an original support, nor fullness of arbitrary other-phase sources. It also does not establish a rectangular-cover implication or prove existence or impossibility of a saturated finite fusion.Minimal exposition correctionsNo additional mathematical hypothesis is needed. I would make these scope clarifications explicit:In §4, say that the first nonfull regular receiver exists by the definition of  $J$  when the cap is full. A full cap alone does not exclude an  $L_3$  stop.In §6, use “positive exterior receiver chain” and “original endpoint-containing phase- $11$  receiver.”If the inherited formula  $C=2J-K_{\mathrm{regular}}$  appears nearby, rename the new route count  $J_{\mathrm{chain}}$  to distinguish it from the older full-tile count.Verification scopeThe reported fixtures exercise the  $J$ -cap alternative and the  $X$ -to- $L_3$  alternative. They do not exercise a  $J$ -route that starts from a full cap and stops later at  $L_3$ . That latter implication is nevertheless proved by the explicit induction above; the absence of a fixture neither refutes it nor establishes that the branch is unrealizable.This verdict is a written mathematical audit.
